articles.body: A dependency upgrade can change more than the function your application imports. It might add an install script, move a command-line entry point, or ship a directory that was absent from the previous release. The changelog gives you the author's explanation. Comparing the two published tarballs shows the changes your application will actually receive. Start with the exact version in your lockfile and the exact proposed replacement. Avoid moving tags such as latest : the review should refer to the same pair of artifacts when a teammate repeats it tomorrow. Keep both archives until the upgrade decision is recorded. Capture both releases in separate directories You need npm and a Linux or WSL shell with tar , sort , diff , and sha512sum .

articles.title: HTML to Markdown API: Clean Markdown From Any Web Page
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I work on APIBox, the API used in this guide. The first draft was written with AI assistance; I tested the code and edited it. Markdown has quietly become the exchange format of the AI era…
articles.body: Disclosure: I work on APIBox, the API used in this guide. The first draft was written with AI assistance; I tested the code and edited it. Markdown has quietly become the exchange format of the AI era. LLMs read it well, it costs far fewer tokens than raw HTML, note apps like Obsidian store it natively, and every static site generator speaks it. The web, however, still ships HTML: navigation bars, cookie banners, inline scripts, tracking pixels and a dozen nested <div> s around three paragraphs of actual content. This guide shows how to use the APIBox /v1/html-to-markdown endpoint to turn HTML strings or live URLs into clean Markdown, and how to wire it into four common jobs: LLM prompts, scrapers, content migration and HTML email.

articles.title: What Is the Difference Between val and var in Kotlin, and Is val Immutable?
articles.excerpt: In short: var can be given a new value. val can't. But val only locks the name, not the object behind it. A val list can still grow, and a val property can return a new value each time you read it. Th…
articles.body: In short: var can be given a new value. val can't. But val only locks the name, not the object behind it. A val list can still grow, and a val property can return a new value each time you read it. That's why Kotlin calls val read-only, not immutable. val stops you from changing the name. It doesn't stop you from changing the thing. Say a search screen shows your recent searches. The state is a data class with val recent: MutableList<String> , kept in a StateFlow . When you search, the code calls recent.add(query) . It compiles, there's a val everywhere, and the list on screen doesn't update. This post covers what val and var really promise, why val isn't immutable, where const val fits, and how to fix that search screen. What is the difference between val and var?

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.
